title: Commit hygiene: amend, and what a good commit looks like
why: Small commits with clear messages make reviews fast and bisect possible. `--amend` fixes the last commit before anyone else has it.
commands:
git status
git add dag.py
git commit --amend -m "add pipeline and dag"   # rewrites the LAST commit
git log --oneline -3
mistake: Never amend a commit you already pushed to a shared branch; others have built on it.
interview: What makes a good commit message? (imperative subject under 50 chars, why in the body, one logical change)

title: Merge conflicts, calmly
why: Two people changed the same lines. Git cannot guess which idea wins, so it marks the region and stops.
commands:
git merge feature            # CONFLICT in report.sql
git status                   # lists conflicted files
# edit: keep the parts you need, delete <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> markers
git add report.sql
git commit                   # finishes the merge
# panic button: git merge --abort
mistake: Resolving by deleting one side without reading it. Always run the code/tests after resolving.
interview: How do you resolve a merge conflict, and how do you reduce how often they happen?

title: Rebase vs merge
why: Rebase replays your commits on top of the new main, giving a straight history that is easy to read and bisect. Merge keeps history exactly as it happened.
commands:
git switch feature
git rebase main               # replay feature commits on top of main
# on conflict: fix, git add, git rebase --continue   (or --abort)
git push --force-with-lease  # only for YOUR feature branch
mistake: Rebasing a branch others use. Golden rule: rebase private branches, merge shared ones.
interview: When do you rebase and when do you merge?

title: Squash messy commits
why: Reviewers want one meaningful commit, not 'wip 1..5'.
commands:
git reset --soft main        # keep all changes, drop the commits
git commit -m "add work file"
# or: git rebase -i main  and mark commits as 'squash'
mistake: Squashing after pushing to a shared branch.
interview: What does git reset --soft vs --mixed vs --hard do?

title: Undo safely: revert vs reset
why: Once a commit is pushed, never rewrite it. `revert` adds a new commit that undoes it.
commands:
git log --oneline
git revert <bad-sha>         # new commit that undoes the bad one
git push
# local-only mistakes: git reset --hard <good-sha>   (destroys uncommitted work!)
mistake: Using reset --hard on a shared branch, or with uncommitted work you wanted.
interview: A bad commit is in production. How do you undo it?

title: Nothing is lost: reflog
why: Every move of HEAD is recorded for ~90 days. Deleted branches and 'lost' commits are usually one command away.
mistake: Panicking and re-cloning, which throws the reflog away.
interview: You deleted a branch with unmerged work. How do you get it back?

title: Stash: switch context without losing work
why: A production bug arrives while your work is half done.
commands:
git stash push -m "half feature"
# fix the hotfix, commit it
git stash list
git stash pop                 # bring the work back (apply + drop)
mistake: Forgetting stashes for weeks. Prefer a WIP commit on a branch for anything longer than an hour.
interview: What is git stash and when would you avoid it?

title: Cherry-pick a hotfix
why: The fix is on main but the release branch must get only that fix.
commands:
git log --oneline main        # find the fix sha
git switch release
git cherry-pick <fix-sha>
# conflicts: resolve, git add, git cherry-pick --continue
mistake: Cherry-picking many commits instead of merging; you lose the link between them.
interview: How do you ship one fix to an older release?

title: Find the breaking commit with bisect
why: A metric went wrong somewhere in the last 50 commits. Bisect finds it in about 6 steps.
commands:
git bisect start HEAD <known-good-sha>
git bisect run ./test.sh      # automatic: exit 0 = good, non-zero = bad
# or manually: git bisect good / git bisect bad
git bisect reset
mistake: Not having a reproducible test; write the 3-line check first.
interview: How would you find which change broke a pipeline?

title: Detached HEAD
why: Checking out a commit (not a branch) puts you in detached HEAD. Commits made there belong to no branch.
commands:
git switch -c rescue          # name the work where you are
git switch main
mistake: Switching away without naming the commits; they become reflog-only.
interview: What is detached HEAD and how do you get out of it?

title: A teammate force-pushed
why: Your commit disappeared from the remote. Do not force-push back; merge their history with yours.
commands:
git fetch
git log --oneline --graph --all
git pull --rebase origin main    # or a merge
git push                          # no --force
# protect main: branch protection, and --force-with-lease if you must
mistake: Answering a force-push with another force-push.

title: A secret was committed
why: Deleting the file in a new commit does not help: it is still in history. Rotate the key first, then rewrite history.
commands:
# 1. ROTATE the key now.
# 2. rewrite history (preferred tool: git filter-repo)
git filter-repo --path .env --invert-paths
# built-in fallback:
git filter-branch --index-filter 'git rm --cached --ignore-unmatch .env' -- --all
echo .env >> .gitignore
# 3. force-push with the team's agreement; ask GitHub support to purge caches
mistake: Thinking a new 'remove .env' commit fixes it.
interview: You pushed an API key to GitHub. What do you do, in order?

title: Conflicts in generated files
why: Lock files, compiled outputs and notebooks conflict badly. Do not hand-merge them; regenerate.
commands:
git merge feature
git checkout --ours lock.json      # take main's version
# re-run the tool that generates it (pip-compile, npm install, dbt deps...)
git add lock.json && git commit
mistake: Hand-editing JSON lock files and shipping a broken environment.
interview: How do you handle conflicts in lock files or notebooks?

title: Worktrees: two branches at once
why: Review a PR or hotfix without stashing your current work.
commands:
git worktree add ../hotfix hotfix
cd ../hotfix && ...commit...
git worktree remove ../hotfix
mistake: Leaving old worktrees around; list them with git worktree list.
interview: How do you work on a hotfix while a long build runs on your branch?

title: Hooks: stop bad commits before they exist
why: A pre-commit hook can block secrets, run formatters and tests.
mistake: Relying on hooks alone; CI must run the same checks because hooks can be skipped.
interview: What would you put in a pre-commit hook for a data repo?

title: The pull-request flow
why: How real teams ship: branch, small commits, push, PR with description, review, squash-merge.
commands:
git switch -c feat/readme
...edit, commit...
git push -u origin feat/readme
gh pr create --fill
gh pr view --web
mistake: Huge PRs. Aim for under 400 lines and one idea.
interview: Walk me through your team's PR process.
